meta.title: Who really said "I Do Not Want to Predict the Future. I Want to Prevent It"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No source documents Frank Herbert saying this. The earliest 1977 attestation credits Ray Bradbury; Herbert's only version is a different, reported sentence.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I Do Not Want to Predict the Future. I Want to Prevent It'?
meta.ogDescription: The first-person line has no Frank Herbert source — it is Quote Investigator's own headline. The earliest 1977 attestation credits Ray Bradbury instead.

answer.label: Not Frank Herbert — the documented first-person versions are all Ray Bradbury’s
answer.sourceLine: No source documents Frank Herbert saying this first-person sentence. The string is, in fact, the headline of Quote Investigator’s article ↗ about the saying — a researcher’s summary, not a transcript. QI’s earliest attestation, Theodore Sturgeon’s 1977 introduction to World Soul, credits Ray Bradbury, and every documented first-person version is Bradbury’s. Herbert’s only version on record is a different, third-person sentence, and even that reaches us as reported speech from his critic Timothy O’Reilly rather than as a quotation.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

source.excerpt: Herbert’s study in the Dune trilogy of the superhero mystique is a good example of this journalistic technique. He has said that the function of science fiction is not always to predict the future but sometimes to prevent it.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the saying from Theodore Sturgeon’s 1977 introduction to World Soul — which credits Ray Bradbury — through Bradbury’s own first-person versions, and concludes that the precise origin is unconfirmed.
The Herbert attribution enters print in 1978, in Timothy O’Reilly’s essay on Dune for Critical Encounters, ed. Dick Riley (Ungar, 1978) ↗, and is repeated in O’Reilly’s 1981 book-length study.

Reading O’Reilly’s text directly ↗ shows the sentence is reported, not quoted — and Wikiquote’s Frank Herbert page ↗ carries no version of the line at all, while Bradbury’s page ↗ carries the first-person form.
source.excerptNote: Read the construction closely. O’Reilly writes “He has said that…” with no quotation marks — and then, one sentence later in the same paragraph, puts Herbert’s genuine words inside quotes. The version travelling the internet in quotation marks is a biographer’s summary that acquired punctuation it never had.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can be asserted for the circulating wording, because no primary source for it has been identified — and quotle.info does not claim public domain for anything it cannot tie to a specific work. Every documented near-wording is far too recent to be free in any case: the Sturgeon introduction (1977), O’Reilly’s two Ungar volumes (1978 and 1981) and Bradbury’s essays and interviews all postdate 1931 and remain in copyright with their authors’ estates and publishers.

author.name: Ray Bradbury
author.kicker: The name the line is actually documented under
author.heading: Who Ray Bradbury was
author.bio: Ray Bradbury (born 22 August 1920, died 5 June 2012) wrote Fahrenheit 451 (1953), The Martian Chronicles and hundreds of short stories, and spent six decades insisting in public that he was not a prophet. The predict-versus-prevent line is the compressed form of that lifelong protest: he repeated it in essays, interviews and lectures, and by 1977 it was already circulating with his name on it. He is the earliest person on record credited with the thought — though Quote Investigator stops short of declaring him its inventor.

misattribution.heading: Where the credit goes wrong
misattribution.intro: This one fails in three separate places at once: the wrong speaker, the wrong wording, and a “quotation” that was never a quotation. Each is worth separating, because two of the three are half-true.

items.why: The first-person sentence is not documented for Herbert anywhere. His only version on record is third-person and about the genre, not himself: “the function of science fiction is not always to predict the future but sometimes to prevent it,” first printed in 1978 ↗. Swapping that for a punchy “I want to prevent it” is not a trim — it changes who the sentence is about.

O’Reilly’s text ↗ reads “He has said that the function of science fiction is not always to predict the future but sometimes to prevent it” — no quotation marks, while Herbert’s actual words are placed in quotes one sentence later. What circulates as a Herbert quotation is a biographer’s paraphrase with quotation marks added afterwards.

The exact string being credited — “I Do Not Want to Predict the Future. I Want to Prevent It” — is the title of the QI article ↗ investigating the saying. The reader who wrote in to QI asked about yet another wording. A research heading is the researcher’s prose; it belongs to no speaker and no year.

QI’s earliest find, Theodore Sturgeon’s 1977 introduction to World Soul, credits Bradbury — and the documented first-person forms are all his. But QI is explicit that the citation points to an earlier origin it cannot reach, and it declines to decide ↗ between Bradbury and Herbert. Neither should be called the coiner.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest summary: Frank Herbert argued the preventive case for science fiction, but not in these words and not in the first person. Quote Investigator ↗ puts the earliest documented credit with Ray Bradbury in 1977 and leaves the ultimate origin open — so we do too.

context.heading: How a critic’s summary became a quotation
lead: Two of American science fiction’s biggest names were born in 1920 — Ray Bradbury in August, Frank Herbert in October — and both spent their careers batting away the word “prophet.” That shared irritation is why this line drifts between them so easily. Bradbury said it in the first person, over and over, for decades. Herbert said something adjacent about what science fiction is for, and it survives only because his critic wrote it down.

The mechanism is worth watching, because it is how a great many “quotes” are manufactured. In his 1981 study, Timothy O’Reilly writes: “He has said that the function of science fiction is not always to predict the future but sometimes to prevent it.” One sentence later, O’Reilly puts Herbert’s actual words inside quotation marks. The omission in the first sentence is deliberate — it is a summary of something Herbert said, not a record of how he said it. Quote sites later supplied the missing quotation marks, and the paraphrase graduated into a quotation.
context.detailsSummary: What Frank Herbert actually wrote about prediction
detailsBody: Herbert did write about prophecy and prediction, at length and in his own voice. In “Dune Genesis,” his essay for Omni (Vol. 2, No. 2, July 1980, p. 72), he wrote: “Do you want an absolute prediction? Then you want only today, and you reject tomorrow. You are the ultimate conservative. You are trying to hold back movement in an infinitely changing universe.” That passage is sourced on Wikiquote ↗; the predict-versus-prevent line is not on that page at all.

The idea attributed to Herbert is also genuinely his in substance. In the same paragraph of O’Reilly’s book, Herbert is quoted directly on Huxley and Orwell: “Neither Brave New World nor 1984 will prevent our becoming a planet under Big Brother’s thumb, but they make it a bit less likely. We’ve been sensitized to the possibility.” That is Herbert, in quotation marks, arguing exactly the preventive case — just not in the words the internet puts in his mouth.
context.pull: “He has said that…” is not a quotation. It is a biographer telling you the gist.

schema.verdictNote: Not documented for Frank Herbert. This exact first-person wording is the headline of Quote Investigator’s article on the saying, not a transcript. The earliest documented credit for the underlying saying is Ray Bradbury — Theodore Sturgeon’s 1977 introduction to World Soul, wording it “The function of science fiction is not only to predict the future, but to prevent it” — but Quote Investigator does not resolve whether Bradbury or Herbert said it first, so this Quotation asserts no creator.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's article is titled "Quote Origin: I Do Not Want to Predict the Future. I Want to Prevent It"; its earliest citation is 1977, Theodore Sturgeon's introduction to Emtsev and Parnov's World Soul (trans. Antonina W. Bouis, Macmillan), crediting Ray Bradbury with "The function of science fiction is not only to predict the future, but to prevent it"; it records Timothy O'Reilly attributing "the function of science fiction is not always to predict the future but sometimes to prevent it" to Frank Herbert in Critical Encounters (ed. Dick Riley, Ungar, 1978), p. 55, and again in O'Reilly's Frank Herbert (Ungar, 1981); it lists Bradbury first-person forms from 1982, 1994 and 1996; and it concludes the precise origin is unconfirmed, without determining whether Bradbury or Herbert said it first.

Chapter 2 ("Under Pressure") of the online edition of Timothy O'Reilly's Frank Herbert contains, without quotation marks, "Herbert's study in the Dune trilogy of the superhero mystique is a good example of this journalistic technique. He has said that the function of science fiction is not always to predict the future but sometimes to prevent it.", followed one sentence later by Herbert's directly quoted remark on Brave New World and 1984.
The online edition of Timothy O'Reilly's Frank Herbert states it was originally published under copyright 1981 by Frederick Ungar Publishing Co., Inc., and lists Chapter 2 as "Under Pressure".

Wikiquote's Frank Herbert page does not contain the predict/prevent line in any section, but does carry a sourced passage on prediction from "Dune Genesis", an essay in Omni, Vol. 2, No. 2 (July 1980), p. 72: "Do you want an absolute prediction? Then you want only today, and you reject tomorrow. You are the ultimate conservative..."

Wikiquote's Ray Bradbury page carries the first-person wording "People ask me to predict the future, when all I want to do is prevent it. Better yet, build it. Predicting the future is much too easy, anyway.", cited to the essay "Beyond 1984: The People Machines".
The Internet Archive holds Critical Encounters: Writers and Themes in Science Fiction, creator Dick Riley, publisher New York: Ungar, dated 1978 — the volume containing O'Reilly's Dune essay.
Frank Herbert was born 8 October 1920 and died 11 February 1986; Dune was first published in 1965.
Ray Bradbury was born 22 August 1920 and died 5 June 2012; Fahrenheit 451 was published in 1953.
